newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Iraq proclaims innocence, blames US for oil delay.
newsitem.headline: Iraq proclaims innocence, blames US for oil delay.

text.p: Protesting its innocence, Iraq on Wednesday demanded that the United Nations implement the oil-for-food deal and stand up to Washington's alleged illegal and sustained campaign against Baghdad.

Iraq's Foreign Minister Mohammed Saeed al-Sahaf told the U.N. General Assembly that the United States had no justification for its recent missile attacks on Iraq and was singly responsible for delaying implementation of the oil-for-food deal that had been agreed on May 20.

The minister also harsly criticized the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) in charge of destroying Iraq's weapons of mass destruction, a prime requirement for lifting six-year old U.N. trade sanctions. He said it had sent 373 inspection teams with 3,574 inspectors in more than five years in addition to a staff of 90 in Baghdad.
"What has this huge army of inspectors been doing for all this long period of time? They did not come to Iraq for a vacation,"

Sahaf demanded that Egypt, which currently has a seat in the 15-member Security Council, participate "directly" in the work and activities of UNSCOM along with the council's permanent members -- the United States, Russia, Britain, France and China.

He said Iraq was not concealing weapons as the commission charged, based on mere suspicions unsupported by material evidence. "They emanate from American and British intelligence services and their agents," he said.
On the oil-for-food plan, he said Washington had put hurdles in the way of each phase of the negotiations between Iraq and the United Nations before and after the agreement was signed.
"Because of U.S. pressure and interference, the secretary-general has until now been unable to implement the memorandum of understanding (on the oil plan)," he said.
"We believe that these acts should cease and that the United Nations Secretariat and Iraq be left to implement the memorandum as soon as possible, without any inteference in the future," he said.

The oil deal plan allows Iraq to enter international oil markets for the first time in six years to sell $ 2 billion worth of crude to purchase food and other necessities for its people suffering under U.N. sanctions. The embargoes were imposed in August 1990 when Baghdad's troops invaded Kuwait.

Sahaf said that President Saddam Hussein's troops went to Kurdish areas in northern Iraq last month to put an end to the civil war, chaos and insecurity, which the United States tried to exploit by missile attacks he said left "many martyrs and wounded civilians."
The United States and Britain then expanded a no-fly zone in southern Iraq which was illegal in the first place and never called for in a Security Council resolution.
"I am wondering here: is a state entitled to forcibly impose such a situation on another independent state...on the pretext of protecting its strategic interests," he asked.
"All the allegations and pretexts put forward by the United States to justify its attacks and military build-up against Iraq have no justification in law, fact or legitimacy," he said,
